The yellowfin notothen Patagonotothen guntheri is a benthic notothenioid fish inhabiting the subantarctic waters of the South American shelf. Field surveys of the species have documented that reproductively active adults achieve a maximum recorded total length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 143 grams [Wwi = 143 grams], a value that corresponds to an asymptotic body form typical of smaller-bodied nototheniids. Females begin the process of sexual maturation relatively slowly, with puberty being attained at a total length of 10.2 centimeters [Lp = 10.2 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 10.7 grams [Wwp = 10.7 grams]. Comparative growth data derived from otolith readings indicate that this size threshold is generally reached at approximately 1277.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 1277.5 days since birth], a pace that aligns with the extended developmental periods observed in cold-adapted notothenioids at a temperature of 6.1 °C [T = 6.1 °C]. The morphological transition from the larval to the juvenile stage, involving fin ray ossification and scale formation, occurs gradually over the first several months of life as individuals recruit to the demersal habitat.

At the time of eclosion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a modest endowment of endogenous reserves. Based on the typical egg diameter of 1.3 millimeters recorded in the congeneric Patagonotothen ramsayi, the calculated wet weight at birth for P. guntheri is approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams]. This extremely small neonatal mass is characteristic of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce numerous, small, yolk-laden ova. Following the absorption of the yolk sac and the onset of exogenous feeding, the free-swimming larva begins a period of rapid mass gain. Juveniles remain in the planktonic larval phase for an extended duration before undergoing larval metamorphosis and settling to the benthos. The ecological transition from the pelagic to the benthic habitat represents a critical bottleneck in the early life history, with mortality rates presumed to be high during this period of habitat shift. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days], or roughly 11 years, at the same thermal regime at a temperature of 6.1 °C [T = 6.1 °C].

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated from fecundity relationships established for the closely related Patagonotothen ramsayi. Under stable thermal conditions of 6.1 °C [T = 6.1 °C], a reproductively active female at the ultimate length of 23 centimeters is capable of producing approximately 54 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 54 eggs per spawning event], with spawning events occurring roughly once per year [F_R_i = roughly once per year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate of approximately 54 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 54 eggs per year] when maintained at 6.1 °C. This level of fecundity is relatively low compared to many other nototheniid species, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes the production of larger, more yolky eggs over sheer numerical output. The interval between successive spawning events is tied to the annual temperature cycle and the availability of suitable spawning substrates on the continental shelf.
